stem: Economic development differs from economic growth because development

options.content: means only a rise in real GDP per head
includes health, education and poverty reduction as well as output
options.rationale: Correct: it is a broader improvement in well-being.

options.content: is measured only by changes in the general level of prices and in wages over time
refers only to a rise in exports and imports
options.rationale: Exports are one part of output.

explanation: Growth is a rise in real output; development includes wider improvements in well-being.

stem: Which statement about real GDP per head is correct?

options.content: It is adjusted for inflation and for the size of the population
It shows how income is shared between households
options.rationale: It is an average and hides inequality.

options.content: It includes the value of unpaid household work
It is the same as nominal GDP divided by the exchange rate of the currency

explanation: Real GDP per head = real GDP ÷ population.

stem: Converting incomes using purchasing power parity rather than market exchange rates is intended to

options.content: allow for differences in the size of populations between the countries compared
options.rationale: That is done by using per head figures.

options.content: remove the effect of inflation over time
options.rationale: That is done by using real values.

options.content: show how equally income is distributed
allow for differences in the prices of goods between countries
options.rationale: Correct: it compares what incomes can buy.

explanation: PPP compares purchasing power rather than currency values.

stem: Which is a reason why GDP per head may overstate the living standard of a typical person in a developing economy?

options.content: It counts unpaid subsistence output at much too high a value in the figures
It includes only the informal sector
options.rationale: The informal sector is partly excluded.

options.content: It is an average, and a few very rich households can raise it
options.rationale: Correct: the mean is affected by high incomes.

options.content: It is always adjusted for the environment

explanation: An average hides the distribution of income.

stem: The Human Development Index combines

options.content: the price level, the unemployment rate and the growth rate
life expectancy, years of schooling and income per head
the Gini coefficient, the inflation rate and the budget deficit
exports, imports and the exchange rate

explanation: The HDI is a geometric mean of health, education and income indices.
hints: Which three dimensions does the HDI cover?

stem: The Kuznets curve suggests that as income per head rises inequality at first

options.content: rises and later falls
falls and later rises
rises continuously
options.rationale: The hypothesis predicts an eventual fall.

options.content: is unaffected
options.rationale: The hypothesis links inequality to income.

explanation: The Kuznets hypothesis predicts an inverted U between inequality and income per head.
hints: Is it a U or an inverted U?

stem: Which is a weakness of the HDI as a measure of development?

options.content: It includes only the level of income per head
options.rationale: It also includes health and education.

options.content: It cannot be compared between countries
It uses nominal rather than real values
options.rationale: The income measure is adjusted for purchasing power.

options.content: It ignores inequality and damage to the environment
options.rationale: Correct: it uses averages and excludes environmental costs.

explanation: The HDI is an average and does not include the environment or freedoms.
hints: What is not in the three dimensions?

stem: The Multidimensional Poverty Index measures

options.content: the share of income received by the richest 10%
the average income of the poorest households only
options.rationale: It is not an income measure.

options.content: the proportion of people deprived in health, education and living standards
the difference in average income between rich and poor countries
options.rationale: It measures poverty within a country.

explanation: The MPI counts deprivations across several dimensions and their intensity.

stem: Distinguish between economic growth and economic development.

points.description: Economic growth is an increase in real output (real GDP or GDP per head) over time
Economic development is a broader improvement in well-being, including health, education and reduction in poverty

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Economic growth is an increase in real output over time, while economic development is a broader improvement in well-being that includes health, education and the reduction of poverty.

explanation: Output against wider well-being.

stem: Explain two limitations of using real GDP per head to compare living standards between countries.

points.description: It is an average and hides inequality in the distribution of income.
So a country with a high average may have many poor people.
It excludes unpaid and subsistence work and much of the informal economy.
So it understates output in countries where these are important (also ignores the environment and leisure).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Real GDP per head is an average and hides inequality, so a country with a high average may have many poor people. It also excludes unpaid and subsistence work and much of the informal economy, so it understates output in countries where these are important.

explanation: Two limitations explained.
hints: Think of what GDP leaves out.

stem: Explain why the Human Development Index may give a different ranking of two countries from GDP per head.

points.description: The HDI includes life expectancy and years of schooling as well as income.
A country with a lower income per head may have better health and education.
The income component uses logarithms, so extra income counts for less at higher levels.
So a poorer country with good health and education may score higher than a richer one.
GDP per head ignores health and education.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The HDI includes life expectancy and years of schooling as well as income, so a country with a lower income per head but better health and education may score higher. The income component uses logarithms, so extra income counts for less at higher levels, whereas GDP per head ignores health and education altogether.

explanation: Wider coverage and diminishing weight of income.

stem:
**Comparing Tamba and Kavala (fictional, illustrative)**

Tamba's GNI per head is 90,000 units of local currency. The market exchange rate is 30 units per US dollar, and the PPP exchange rate is 20 units per US dollar. Data for Tamba and Kavala are shown below.

| Country | GNI per head, market rate (US\$) | PPP-adjusted GNI per head (US\$) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Tamba | 3,000 | 4,500 |
| Kavala | 3,600 | 3,900 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate Tamba's GNI per head in US dollars at the market exchange rate.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate Tamba's GNI per head in US dollars at the PPP exchange rate.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: By what percentage is Tamba's PPP-adjusted GNI per head higher than Kavala's? Give your answer to one decimal place.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain why Tamba's PPP income is higher than its income at the market exchange rate.

points.description: The prices of many goods and services are lower in Tamba than in countries where the market rate is used for comparison.
So each US dollar of income buys more in Tamba.
The PPP rate (20) is lower than the market rate (30), reflecting this lower price level.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Prices of many goods and services, especially non-traded ones, are lower in Tamba than in the countries used for comparison, so each dollar of income buys more there. The PPP rate of 20 units to the dollar is lower than the market rate of 30, which reflects this lower price level, so the PPP income is higher.

explanation: Market-rate US\$3,000; PPP US\$4,500; 15.4% higher than Kavala; lower local prices explain the difference.
hints: Local GNI ÷ exchange rate gives US dollars at the market rate.

stem:
**Measuring development in Mbira (fictional, illustrative)**

Mbira has a life expectancy of 66 years, mean years of schooling of 8, expected years of schooling of 12 and GNI per head of US\$4,500. Its income index is 0.575 (calculated from the logarithm formula). Mbira has a large informal sector and a very unequal distribution of income, and its mining industry has damaged the environment. The government says that the country is developing quickly because GNI per head has risen.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate Mbira's health index, to three decimal places.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate Mbira's education index, to three decimal places.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Using the income index of 0.575, calculate Mbira's HDI, to three decimal places.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Assess whether the HDI is a better measure than GNI per head of whether Mbira is developing.

points.description: The HDI includes health and education as well as income, so it shows whether people's lives are improving.
GNI per head is a single, easily available figure but an average that hides inequality.
Neither measure includes inequality in Mbira's distribution, the informal sector or the environmental damage from mining.
The HDI weights the three dimensions equally and income is logarithmic, so it is less affected by very high incomes.
Other indicators (MPI, MEW, inequality measures) would give a fuller picture.
Judgement.

levels.descriptor: Two-sided, developed and applied to the data, with a supported judgement.
Some development of one side or limited use of the data.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The HDI is better than GNI per head because it includes life expectancy and years of schooling, so it shows whether people's health and education are improving alongside income, and its logarithmic income index reduces the effect of very high incomes. GNI per head is simpler and easily available, but it is an average that hides inequality and ignores health and education. However, neither measure includes Mbira's very unequal distribution of income, the informal sector, or the environmental damage from mining, so the government's claim of rapid development is not proven by either figure. The HDI is therefore a better single guide, but a fuller assessment would use other indicators such as the MPI or a measure of inequality.

explanation: Health 0.708; education 0.600; HDI 0.625; the HDI is broader than GNI per head but still omits inequality and the environment.
hints: In (d) consider what each measure includes and leaves out.

stem: Assess whether real GDP per head is a reliable measure of the standard of living in a developing economy.

points.description: It adjusts for inflation and population and is available regularly.
It is an average and hides inequality.
It excludes subsistence output, unpaid work and much of the informal economy.
It ignores leisure, environmental damage and the quality of goods.
Prices differ between countries, so PPP is needed for comparison.
Non-monetary indicators (life expectancy, schooling) and composite indices (HDI) add information.
Real GDP per head is useful for trends over time within one country.
A justified judgement.

levels.descriptor: Two-sided, applied and developed, with a justified conclusion.
Some development of one or both sides, limited application or conclusion.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Real GDP per head is useful because it is adjusted for inflation and population and is available regularly, so it can show trends in average incomes. However, it is only an average and hides inequality, and it excludes subsistence output, unpaid work and much of the informal economy, which are large in developing economies. It also ignores leisure and environmental damage, and market exchange rates can misrepresent purchasing power, so PPP is needed for comparisons between countries. Non-monetary indicators such as life expectancy and schooling and composite indices such as the HDI add important information. Overall it is a useful starting point but not a reliable measure of the standard of living on its own.

explanation: Weigh availability and comparability against averages, omissions and the environment.
hints: Consider what money measures leave out and what composite measures add.
